title: Respiratory Virus Testing: Molecular vs Antigen vs Culture
summary: Compare the glance of an antigen test, the photocopier of a NAAT and the greenhouse of viral culture — and learn why a negative rapid test in flu season needs a molecular follow-up.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 64 Hit 1 (core: molecular testing for respiratory viruses) and the Figure 64 memory anchor, using influenza as the worked example. The reviewer’s “multiplex NAATs are the standard of care” is narrowed to the IDSA 2018 recommendations (multiplex panels for hospitalized immunocompromised patients); see register flag rv-multiplex-soc.

objectives: Compare antigen tests, molecular assays and viral culture by target, speed and sensitivity.
Explain why amplification makes NAATs more sensitive and what multiplex panels add.
Choose influenza tests by patient group and interpret a negative rapid antigen test.

scenes.title: A negative rapid test in flu season
scenes.altText: Peak influenza season. A feverish, coughing patient has a rapid antigen test: one control line, no test line — negative. A tempting token “Not influenza” appears and then gets a question mark.

cues.text: It’s the peak of flu season. A patient has fever and cough, and a rapid antigen test comes back negative.
Does that rule out influenza? Many people would say yes.
It doesn’t. To see why, compare the three ways a lab can look for a virus.

scenes.title: Normal: three ways to find a virus
scenes.altText: Three lanes. Antigen test: detects viral proteins, results in 10–15 minutes, moderate sensitivity (about 50–70%) and high specificity (over 90%). Molecular test (NAAT, e.g. RT-PCR): detects viral nucleic acid; rapid molecular assays about 90–95% sensitive, RT-PCR very high sensitivity and specificity. Viral culture: grows live virus in cells; shell-vial culture 1–3 days, traditional culture 3–10 days; allows detailed antigenic and genetic characterization.

cues.text: An antigen test looks for viral proteins. It’s fast — 10 to 15 minutes — and specific, but only moderately sensitive: about 50 to 70 percent.
A molecular test, or NAAT, such as RT-PCR, looks for the virus’s genetic material. Rapid molecular assays are about 90 to 95 percent sensitive; RT-PCR is very sensitive and specific.
Viral culture grows live virus in cells. It takes 1 to 3 days with shell vials, or 3 to 10 days traditionally.
Culture is slow, but it lets reference labs characterize the virus in detail.

scenes.title: What changes: copying the evidence
scenes.altText: A single strand of viral nucleic acid is copied over and over: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 copies, the count climbing cycle by cycle until it crosses a detection line. Beside it, an antigen strip needs many viral proteins to make a visible line; with few viruses the line never appears. Sensitivity bars grow: antigen ~50–70%, rapid molecular ~90–95%. Then one swab feeds a multiplex panel whose wells light up for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 and other targets.

cues.text: Why are molecular tests so much more sensitive? They copy the evidence. Each cycle doubles the target: one copy becomes two, then four, eight, sixteen — until there’s enough to detect.
An antigen test can’t copy anything. It needs a lot of viral protein in the sample to make a visible line, so lower amounts are missed.
That’s the gap in sensitivity: roughly 50 to 70 percent for antigen tests, against about 90 to 95 percent for rapid molecular assays.
A multiplex panel takes it further: one swab, many targets at once — influenza A and B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 and other respiratory pathogens.

scenes.title: In the lab: which test, for whom
scenes.altText: A guideline board (IDSA 2018 influenza guideline) fills in: outpatients — rapid molecular assays over rapid antigen tests; hospitalized patients — RT-PCR or other molecular assays; hospitalized immunocompromised patients — multiplex RT-PCR respiratory panels. Two crossed-out cards: “Culture for initial diagnosis” (results not timely) and “Serology for diagnosis” (a single serum specimen can’t be reliably interpreted). A last token: culture still matters for virus characterization and surveillance.

cues.text: For influenza, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends rapid molecular assays over rapid antigen tests for outpatients.
For hospitalized patients: RT-PCR or other molecular assays.
And for hospitalized patients with weakened immune systems: multiplex RT-PCR panels that test many respiratory pathogens at once.
Don’t use viral culture for the initial diagnosis — the result comes too late. And don’t use serology: a single serum sample can’t be reliably interpreted.
Culture still has a job: it lets public-health labs characterize circulating viruses.

props.label: Outpatients: rapid molecular over rapid antigen
Hospitalized: RT-PCR or other molecular assays

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Negative rapid antigen test = not influenza” is crossed out → “Antigen tests miss many cases; confirm negatives with a molecular test, especially at peak season.” Trap card: “Culture is the gold standard, so order it first” is crossed out → “Too slow for the initial diagnosis; use a molecular test.”

cues.text: Trap one: a negative rapid antigen test does not rule out influenza. Because antigen tests are less sensitive, confirm a negative with a molecular test — especially when flu is peaking in the community.
Trap two: culture is not the first test to order. It is too slow for the initial diagnosis. A molecular test answers the question in time to act.
And remember the trade-off: antigen tests are specific, so a positive is usually believable; it’s the negatives that need care.

scenes.title: Glance, photocopier, greenhouse
scenes.altText: Memory aid: three detectives. The Glance (antigen): quick look, misses quiet suspects. The Photocopier (NAAT): copies tiny clues until they can’t be missed. The Greenhouse (culture): grows the suspect — slow, but you can study it. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: antigen is a glance — quick, but it misses quiet suspects. A NAAT is a photocopier — it copies tiny clues until they can’t be missed. Culture is a greenhouse — it grows the suspect slowly, so you can study it.

Where it breaks: sensitivities vary by assay, virus, specimen and timing; NAATs can stay positive after the infection is over; and recommendations differ by patient group and pathogen. Check the current guideline.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Antigen fast but ~50–70% sensitive”, “Molecular (NAAT) ~90–95%+ · multiplex panels for many targets”, “Culture too slow for initial diagnosis”.

cues.text: Molecular tests detect respiratory viruses far more sensitively than antigen tests, so confirm a negative antigen result with a NAAT, and keep slow viral culture for characterization rather than first diagnosis.

props.label: Culture: too slow for initial diagnosis

explanation.what: Plain language: labs can look for a virus’s proteins, copy its genetic material, or grow it. Scientific terms: rapid antigen tests (RIDTs) detect viral antigens in 10–15 minutes with moderate sensitivity (~50–70%) and high specificity (> 90%); molecular assays (NAATs such as RT-PCR) detect viral nucleic acid with high (rapid molecular ~90–95%) to very high sensitivity; culture grows virus in 1–3 days (shell vial) to 3–10 days (traditional).
explanation.why: Amplification lets NAATs detect small amounts of nucleic acid that antigen tests miss. Multiplex panels test one specimen for many respiratory pathogens. Culture is too slow for initial diagnosis but supports antigenic and genetic characterization.
explanation.measure: IDSA 2018: rapid molecular assays over RIDTs in outpatients; RT-PCR or other molecular assays in hospitalized patients; multiplex RT-PCR respiratory panels in hospitalized immunocompromised patients; no viral culture for initial diagnosis; no serology. CDC: consider confirming negative RIDTs with molecular assays, especially at peak activity.
explanation.differs: Antigen (fast, specific, insensitive) vs NAAT (sensitive, specific) vs culture (slow, allows characterization); single-target vs multiplex molecular testing.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the most sensitive test for respiratory viruses, why a negative rapid antigen test doesn’t exclude influenza, culture’s limited role in initial diagnosis, and when multiplex panels are recommended.

questions.stem: During peak influenza season, a hospitalized adult with fever and cough has a negative rapid influenza antigen test. What is the best next step?

options.text: Test with RT-PCR or another molecular assay
options.rationale: Correct. Antigen tests are only moderately sensitive; molecular assays are recommended for hospitalized patients and to confirm negatives.
Incorrect. A negative antigen test can miss many infections, especially at peak season.

options.text: Send a viral culture as the main diagnostic test
options.rationale: Incorrect. Culture results are not timely enough for initial diagnosis.
Incorrect. A single serum sample cannot be reliably interpreted for diagnosis.

questions.stem: Why are nucleic acid amplification tests more sensitive than antigen tests for respiratory viruses?

options.text: They copy the viral nucleic acid many times before detection
options.rationale: Correct. Amplification makes small amounts of target detectable.

options.text: They detect antibodies made by the patient
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes serology, not NAAT.

options.text: They grow the virus in cell culture
They use antibodies that bind viral proteins

questions.stem: According to the IDSA 2018 influenza guideline, for which patients are multiplex RT-PCR panels targeting many respiratory pathogens specifically recommended?

options.rationale: Correct. The guideline recommends multiplex RT-PCR panels in this group (A-III).

options.text: All healthy outpatients with a cold
options.rationale: Incorrect. For outpatients the guideline recommends rapid molecular assays over antigen tests, not routine multiplex panels.

options.text: Only patients with a positive antigen test
options.rationale: Incorrect. Panel use is not tied to a positive antigen result.
Incorrect. They are recommended for hospitalized immunocompromised patients.
